609: \section{Conclusion}
610: \label{sec:conclusion}
611: 
612: We argued that the LLM inside a RAG pipeline needs language skills---not
613: world knowledge---and that these skills scale weakly with model size.
614: Three lines of evidence: CheGeKa scales 21.1$\times$ vs.\ 4$\times$ for
615: MultiQ (Figure~\ref{tab:hypothesis}); extraction LLMs from 3\,B to 14\,B
616: yield nearly identical GraphRAG-Bench quality
617: (Table~\ref{tab:gen_medical}); and \menolite{} (7\,B) outperforms
618: Qwen2.5-32B on KG construction (Table~\ref{tab:nerel}).
619: \ragu{} operationalizes these insights via a modular pipeline with
620: 2--4$\times$ higher AC than LightRAG, while HippoRAG\,2 retains an edge on
621: multi-hop reasoning via personalized PageRank.
622: \ragu{} combines competitive quality with engineering maturity and
623: single-GPU deployment. Both artifacts will be released under Apache\,2.0.
624: 
625: % ===================================================================
626: \section*{Limitations}
627: 
628: % \paragraph{Language/world knowledge hypothesis.}
629: % Our empirical evidence (Section~\ref{sec:hypothesis}) draws on one model family (Qwen2.5) and two MERA tasks.
630: % While the pattern is consistent across six model sizes, we cannot rule out that other families or task pairs would behave differently.
631: % MultiQ scores do grow with size---the effect is a markedly shallower scaling curve, not a flat plateau.
632: % We frame this as a hypothesis supported by preliminary evidence, not a proven theorem.
633: 
634: First, our scaling evidence rests on a single model family and select tasks; although robust across model sizes, it is a well-supported hypothesis rather than a universal theorem, and our benchmarks were not specifically tailored to GraphRAG, which may limit analytical granularity.
635: 
636: % \paragraph{Our model.}
637: % The model deliberately trades factual recall for context-grounded skills and should not be used as a standalone knowledge base.
638: % Complex reasoning performance degrades at very long contexts ($>$32K tokens), consistent with other 7\,B-class models.
639: % While the NEREL test set was held out during training, the model was exposed to the NEREL annotation schema and text domain during SFT, which may confer a distributional advantage on our IE benchmark.
640: 
641: Second, \menolite{} trades parametric factual recall for contextual grounding and should not serve as a standalone knowledge base; its multi-hop reasoning degrades beyond 32K tokens, typical of 7\,B-class models. We also note a distributional-overlap caveat on our IE benchmark (Appendix~\ref{app:ie_benchmark}): the supervised fine-tuning of \menolite{} uses the train and validation splits of NEREL, whereas the benchmark uses only the held-out NEREL test split, and the two employ different instruction wordings; furthermore, the benchmark's definition tasks underwent additional LLM-as-judge filtering that the SFT data did not. The overlap is therefore confined to the annotation schema (entity and relation types) and the text domain, not to the benchmark documents, their instruction phrasings, or the reference-quality pipeline---but a residual advantage cannot be fully ruled out.
642: 
643: % \paragraph{Our system.}
644: % The default NetworkX-based graph storage does not scale to very large corpora (millions of nodes); production deployments would require a dedicated graph database.
645: % Graph quality depends heavily on the extraction LLM: weaker models produce noisier entity and relation sets that even the consolidation stage cannot fully recover.
646: 
647: % \paragraph{Experiments.}
648: % On GraphRAG-Bench, we compare \ragu{} directly against LightRAG and other systems under identical conditions.
649: % As discussed in Section~\ref{sec:multihop}, \ragu{} and HippoRAG\,2 exhibit complementary strengths.
650: % The multi-hop QA benchmarks were not specifically designed for GraphRAG evaluation, which may limit analytical sensitivity.
651: % Our engineering observations reflect the state of open-source frameworks at the time of writing (mid-2026).
652: 
653: Finally, \ragu{}'s engineering entails scalability and model dependencies: the default NetworkX graph backend---a swappable \texttt{BaseGraphStorage} adapter rather than a structural coupling---does not by itself scale to massive corpora (millions of nodes), so such deployments require a dedicated graph-database adapter, and final graph quality remains sensitive to the extraction LLM, as weak base models introduce structural noise that consolidation cannot fully rectify.
654:

659: \menolite{} was trained on publicly available datasets (FineWeb-Edu, RuLM,
660: NEREL, MultiHop-RAG, MTRAGEval) and synthetic GPT-4o-mini instructions;

1000: \section{IE Benchmark Definition}
1001: \label{app:ie_benchmark}
1002: 
1003: This appendix documents the information-extraction (IE) benchmark
1004: underlying Table~\ref{tab:nerel}, making its construction, sizes, and
1005: metrics fully reproducible. The dataset~\cite{nerel_bench_anon} is released under an MIT license
1006: (dataset and task-implementation links are anonymized for double-blind
1007: review).
1008: 
1009: \paragraph{Provenance and construction.}
1010: The benchmark is a test-only derivative of the NEREL-instruct
1011: dataset~\cite{nerel_instruct_anon}, which reformats the human-annotated
1012: NEREL corpus~\cite{loukachevitch2021nerel} into an instruction-tuning
1013: layout. Only the \emph{test} split of NEREL is retained; no training or
1014: validation documents appear, so the benchmark documents are disjoint from
1015: the supervised fine-tuning data of \menolite{}
1016: (Appendix~\ref{app:training}). The benchmark comprises four generation
1017: tasks---entity recognition (NER), entity definition (Def), relation
1018: extraction (RE), and relation definition (RDef)---each posing a
1019: knowledge-graph-construction sub-problem rather than a classification
1020: slot. All four are integrated into the LM Evaluation
1021: Harness~\cite{evalharness2024} under the \texttt{nerel-bench} tag,
1022: enabling standardized evaluation of any causal LLM. The full prompts are
1023: listed in Appendix~\ref{app:prompts}.
1024: 
1025: \begin{table}[!t]
1026: \centering
1027: \small
1028: \caption{IE benchmark configurations. ``Abbr.'' is the column header used
1029: in Table~\ref{tab:nerel}. \#test is the number of examples in the test
1030: split.}
1031: \label{tab:ie_bench_configs}
1032: \begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}l l X c@{}}
1033: \toprule
1034: Task & Abbr. & Description & \#test \\
1035: \midrule
1036: entity\_recognition  & NER  & List all entities in the text in normalized form                & 64   \\
1037: entity\_definition   & Def  & Generate a context-grounded definition of a single entity       & 1077 \\
1038: relation\_extraction & RE   & List the entities directly related to a given target entity     & 1452 \\
1039: relation\_definition & RDef & Explain the relation between a pair of entities in context      & 1313 \\
1040: \midrule
1041: \multicolumn{3}{@{}l}{Total} & 3906 \\
1042: \bottomrule
1043: \end{tabularx}
1044: \end{table}
1045: 
1046: \paragraph{Shared normalization.}
1047: Before any metric is computed, both predictions and references are passed
1048: through a shared normalizer~$\nu$: (i)~lowercasing and whitespace
1049: trimming; (ii)~tokenization with \texttt{nltk.wordpunct\_tokenize},
1050: keeping only alphanumeric tokens, which strips the quotation marks and
1051: brackets that NEREL uses inconsistently around entity mentions;
1052: (iii)~Snowball stemming for Russian, which reduces inflectional variants
1053: (case, gender, number, tense) to a common stem. Stemming is essential
1054: for Russian, where a single proper noun can surface in over a dozen
1055: grammatical forms depending on its syntactic role, and all such forms
1056: should match a single reference entity. In the extraction tasks, $\nu$ is
1057: applied per line (entities are newline-separated); in the definition
1058: tasks, $\nu$ is applied to the whole output string.
1059: 
1060: \paragraph{F1 metric (NER, RE).}
1061: For extraction tasks we report set-based \emph{micro-averaged}~$F_1$.
1062: Let $P_i$ and $R_i$ denote the sets of normalized predicted and reference
1063: entities for example~$i$:
1064: \begin{equation}
1065: P = \frac{\sum_i |P_i \cap R_i|}{\sum_i |P_i|}, \qquad
1066: R = \frac{\sum_i |P_i \cap R_i|}{\sum_i |R_i|}, \qquad
1067: F_1 = \frac{2\,P\,R}{P + R}.
1068: \label{eq:f1}
1069: \end{equation}
1070: Micro-averaging treats every entity equally regardless of its document,
1071: so a long text containing many entities contributes proportionally more
1072: to the score.
1073: 
1074: \paragraph{chrF++ metric (Def, RDef).}
1075: For free-form definition generation we report chrF++
1076: \cite{popovic2015chrf,popovic2017chrfpp} computed with the
1077: \texttt{sacrebleu} toolkit~\cite{post2018sacrebleu}. chrF is the
1078: $F_\beta$ score over character $n$-grams ($n{=}1\ldots 6$), and chrF++
1079: augments it with word $n$-grams ($n{=}1,2$) so that multi-word entity
1080: names and relation phrases are preserved:
1081: \begin{equation}
1082: \mathrm{chrF}_{++} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{D}}
1083:   \frac{1}{100}\,\mathrm{chrF}_{++}\!\bigl(\nu(\hat{y}_i),\,\nu(y_i)\,;\,\beta{=}2\bigr),
1084: \label{eq:chrfpp}
1085: \end{equation}
1086: where $\hat{y}_i$ and $y_i$ are the prediction and reference for
1087: example~$i$, and $\mathrm{chrF}_{++}(\cdot,\cdot)$ denotes
1088: \texttt{sacrebleu.sentence\_chrf} with \texttt{char\_order=6},
1089: \texttt{word\_order=2}, $\beta{=}2$ (the sacrebleu defaults). The score is
1090: \emph{macro-averaged} over the test set and rescaled to~$[0,1]$. We
1091: prefer chrF++ over exact match because a semantically correct Russian
1092: definition routinely differs from the reference in word form, word order,
1093: or lexical choice while remaining valid. Note that F1
1094: (Equation~\ref{eq:f1}) is micro-averaged whereas chrF++
1095: (Equation~\ref{eq:chrfpp}) is macro-averaged; this asymmetry is inherited
1096: from the official LM Evaluation Harness implementation.
1097: 
1098: \paragraph{Annotation quality and filtering.}
1099: The two extraction tasks (NER, RE) inherit their references
1100: \emph{algorithmically} from the gold NEREL annotations via a deterministic
1101: transformation into the instruction format; no LLM is used to generate or
1102: filter their references, so their quality is that of the original NEREL
1103: human annotation~\cite{loukachevitch2021nerel}. The two definition tasks
1104: (Def, RDef) have free-form references that are LLM-generated and therefore
1105: underwent a stringent two-stage filter: GPT-4o-mini was used as an
1106: LLM-as-judge to score every candidate reference against its source text,
1107: and only the top-scoring candidates were retained; a subsequent manual
1108: pass removed the few remaining problematic items.
1109: Table~\ref{tab:ie_bench_quality} reports the retention rates. The contrast
1110: is informative: the F1-scored columns of Table~\ref{tab:nerel} rest on
1111: unaltered gold annotations with no LLM in the loop, whereas the
1112: chrF++-scored columns rest on filtered LLM references---a distinction to
1113: keep in mind when comparing scores across columns.
1114:

1116: \centering
1117: \small
1118: \caption{Annotation provenance and LLM-as-judge retention for the four
1119: IE benchmark tasks.}
1120: \label{tab:ie_bench_quality}
1121: \begin{tabular}{@{}l l l r@{}}
1122: \toprule
1123: Task & Reference source & Judge filter & \#kept /\,pool \\
1124: \midrule
1125: NER  & gold NEREL (algorithmic)             & none                       & ---                       \\
1126: Def  & LLM-generated, judge-filtered        & GPT-4o-mini                & 1077 / 3483 \;(31\%)      \\
1127: RE   & gold NEREL (algorithmic)             & none                       & ---                       \\
1128: RDef & LLM-generated, judge-filtered        & GPT-4o-mini, then manual   & 1313 / 3073 \;(43\%)      \\
1129: \bottomrule
1130: \end{tabular}
1131: \end{table}

1133: \paragraph{Reproducibility.}
1134: Any causal LLM can be evaluated through the LM Evaluation

65: entities and brittle retrieval.
66: We start from a simple observation: the capabilities required of an LLM
67: inside a RAG pipeline---comprehension, extraction, and reasoning over
68: context---are language skills that, unlike factual world knowledge, grow
69: only weakly with model size.
70: This insight yields two contributions.
71: First, a compact 7\,B model optimized for language skills rather than
72: factual recall, which outperforms Qwen2.5-32B on knowledge-graph
73: construction (a +12.5\% relative gain in harmonic mean on our
74: information-extraction benchmark) and matches a same-size general model
75: on English GraphRAG tasks.
76: Second, a modular GraphRAG engine that separates extraction from
77: consolidation: entities and relations pass through two-stage extraction,
78: DBSCAN-backed deduplication, LLM summarization, and hierarchical Leiden
79: community detection before indexing.
80: On GraphRAG-Bench (Medical), our engine improves answer correctness by up
81: to 4$\times$ over LightRAG across four difficulty levels while raising
82: evidence recall from 0.71 to 0.84.
83: A size ablation shows that extraction LLMs from 3\,B to 14\,B yield nearly
84: identical downstream quality, confirming the language-knowledge hypothesis.
85: Model, engine, and the new information-extraction benchmark are released
86: under Apache\,2.0 (links anonymized for review).
87: \end{abstract}
88: 
89: % ===================================================================
90: \section{Introduction}
91: \label{sec:intro}
92: 
93: Retrieval-augmented generation~(RAG) has become the standard paradigm for
94: grounding large language models (LLMs) in external knowledge~\cite{lewis2020rag,gao2023rag_survey}.
95: Traditional RAG systems split documents into flat chunks, embed them in a
96: vector space, and retrieve the top-$k$ at query time---an approach that cannot
97: capture the relational structure connecting entities across documents.
98: Graph RAG~(GraphRAG) addresses this by building a knowledge graph from the
99: corpus and using graph traversal during
100: retrieval~\cite{edge2024graphrag,guo2025lightrag,gutierrez2025hipporag2}.
101: Despite conceptual advances, practical adoption faces three obstacles.
102: 
103: \paragraph{Obstacle 1: Single-pass extraction.}
104: Current GraphRAG systems treat knowledge graph construction as a single LLM
105: extraction pass, producing noisy, duplicated entities with no mechanism to
106: \emph{consolidate} information across chunks.
107: 
108: \paragraph{Obstacle 2: Dependence on expensive LLMs.}
109: Because extraction quality directly determines graph quality, practitioners
110: default to large API models (GPT-4-class), making GraphRAG expensive.
111: This dependence rests on a false premise: the capabilities an LLM needs
112: \emph{inside} a RAG pipeline---comprehension, extraction, reasoning over
113: provided context---are \emph{language skills}, not factual recall.
114: As Section~\ref{sec:hypothesis} shows, language skills grow only weakly
115: with model size, while world knowledge scales steeply.
116: A compact, skill-oriented model is therefore sufficient.
117: 
118: \paragraph{Obstacle 3: Engineering immaturity.}
119: Several open-source frameworks suffer from installation failures or
120: inconsistent APIs.\footnote{During benchmarking, we encountered frameworks
121:   that could not be installed without manual patching.
122:   LightRAG~\cite{guo2025lightrag} is a notable exception.}
123: A GraphRAG engine should be both \emph{semantically} strong and
124: \emph{engineerable}: installable, maintainable, and deployable on
125: cost-effective hardware.
126: 
127: We address all three obstacles with two artifacts:
128: \menolite{}, a 7\,B model fine-tuned from
129: RuadaptQwen2.5-7B-Lite-Beta~\cite{tihomirov2025ruadapt_model} for
130: RAG-oriented language skills, and \ragu{}, a modular GraphRAG engine whose
131: pipeline separates extraction from consolidation---chunking, entity/relation
132: extraction, DBSCAN-backed summarization, Leiden community detection, and
133: community summarization.
134: 
135: Our contributions are:
136: \begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
137:   \item We articulate and empirically validate the \emph{language/world
138:         knowledge hypothesis}: world knowledge scales markedly with model
139:         size, whereas language skills---all that a RAG-internal LLM
140:         requires---do not, justifying compact extractor models
141:         (Section~\ref{sec:hypothesis}).
142:   \item \menolite{}, a 7\,B domain-adapted LLM optimized for language skills
143:         (information extraction, multi-hop reasoning, summarization) that
144:         rivals models up to $\sim$4$\times$ larger on knowledge graph
145:         construction.
146:   \item \ragu{}, an engineering-mature, modular multi-step GraphRAG engine
147:         that separates extraction from consolidation, yielding cleaner and
148:         more connected knowledge graphs.
149:   \item Extensive evaluation under fixed conditions across four GraphRAG
150:         benchmarks (GraphRAG-Bench, BioASQ, MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA)
151:         and three Russian language benchmarks (MERA, LIBRA, and our own
152:         information-extraction benchmark based on the NEREL schema).
153:         Both artifacts will be released under Apache\,2.0.\footnote{Anonymized
154:         code and model links are provided in supplementary materials.}
155: \end{enumerate}
156: 
157: % ===================================================================
158: \section{The Language/World Knowledge Hypothesis}
159: \label{sec:hypothesis}
160: 
161: We hypothesize that \textbf{world knowledge}---facts, entities, and their
162: relationships---scales (near-)linearly with parameter count, whereas
163: \textbf{language skills}---comprehension, extraction, inference over provided
164: context---scale markedly more slowly with parameter count.
165: If so, a RAG pipeline (where external knowledge comes from the retrieval
166: subsystem) should function well with a compact, skill-oriented model.
167: 
168: \paragraph{Motivating experiment.}
169: We evaluate the Qwen2.5-Instruct family~\cite{yang2024qwen2} (0.5\,B--72\,B) on
170: two MERA~\cite{fenogenova2024mera} tasks:
171: \emph{CheGeKa}~\cite{taktasheva-etal-2022-tape} (quiz-style QA requiring world
172: knowledge) and \emph{MultiQ} (multi-hop QA where all facts are in-context).

Перенести исходник рисунка **выше точки ссылки**, чтобы LaTeX встретил его при вёрстке страницы 2 и тогда отложил бы на верх страницы 3 — ровно туда, где находится ссылка. Конкретно:

1. Вырезать блок `\begin{figure*}[t]…\end{figure*}` (`main.tex:241-250`).
2. Вставить его сразу после `\subsection{Multi-Step Graph Construction}\label{sec:pipeline}` (`main.tex:218`), перед предложением «Our pipeline processes documents…».
3. Попутно сменить спецификатор `[t]` → `[!t]` (`!` заставляет LaTeX игнорировать параметры вроде `topfraction`, если бы они блокировали размещение — безвредно, страховка).

**Ожидаемый результат:** рисунок встанет в верх страницы 3, а текст Step 1/Step 2 (со ссылкой «(Figure 2)») окажется прямо под ним — на той же странице. Идеальное размещение.

# Оценка рисков

- **Лимит 6 страниц:** площадь рисунка постоянна (та же, что на стр. 4 сейчас) — общая длина тела не меняется, Ethics должен остаться на стр. 6. Пагинация внутри слегка сдвинется, но это нейтрально. Проверю после пересборки.
- **Ссылки:** `\label{fig:architecture}` остаётся внутри блока, все 4 вызова `\ref` (включая `main.tex:1326, 1463, 1504` в приложениях) резолвятся как раньше.
- **Контент:** ничего не меняется — только позиция исходника поплавка.

**Процесс:** переношу блок + `[!t]` → пересборка → проверяю, что рисунок на стр. 3 (рядом со ссылкой), тело всё ещё в 6 страниц, новых Overfull/undefined нет.
